title: A 3-Million-Year-Old Child Shakes Up the Human Family Tree
summary:
A century after a small fossil skull changed what scientists thought about where humans came from, that same fossil is shaking things up again. A new study in Nature dates the Taung Child, found in South Africa in 1924, to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago. It was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of Vrije Universiteit Brussel.

The Taung Child gave scientists the first solid evidence that humans originated in Africa, and it became the fossil that defined the species Australopithecus africanus. But scientists never set clear rules for deciding which later fossils belonged to that species. Today, the Taung Child is the only fossil that can be identified with certainty as Australopithecus africanus.

Researchers compared it with other early human relatives by studying tooth structure and how brains and teeth developed as it grew. Several adult fossils long grouped into the same species grew in different ways. The differences in brain development suggest they may actually be several different species living around the Sterkfontein region, at the same time or in different periods.

Climate may explain the tangle. Millions of years ago, southern Africa swung between wetter and drier periods, reshaping the landscape again and again. As habitats grew and shrank, groups moved, became separated, and evolved along different paths. Some later met again and interbred.

Fossilized pollen adds another surprise: the Taung Child lived in a much wetter, more forested landscape than the region has today, with tree species now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast.

"For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," says Macho. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk -- it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts."
why_it_matters: The Taung Child is the fossil that first showed humans began in Africa, so sorting out which fossils belong to its species rewrites the story of where we all come from.

background_read: The Taung Child is a small fossil skull of a young early human relative, found in South Africa, that gave scientists the first solid evidence that humans originated in Africa.
It became the fossil that defined the species Australopithecus africanus, but scientists never set clear rules for deciding which later fossils belonged to that species.
A new study looks at this famous fossil again, comparing how its teeth and brain grew with other early human relatives to sort out which fossils truly belong together.
The work also looks at ancient climate and fossil pollen to rebuild the landscape the Taung Child lived in, which was much wetter and more forested than the region is today.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A century after the Taung Child changed ideas about human origins, a new study in Nature dates it to 2.96 to 3.03 million years ago.
KEY EVENT: The study finds the Taung Child may be the only certain Australopithecus africanus, and other fossils grouped with it may be several different species.
├─ WHO: Professor Gabriele Macho of Vrije Universiteit Brussel led the study
├─ WHEN: The Taung Child was found in South Africa in 1924 and lived 2.96 to 3.03 million years ago
└─ WHERE: The fossils come from around the Sterkfontein region in South Africa
EVIDENCE: Tooth structure and brain development differ among fossils long grouped as one species, and fossilized pollen shows a wetter, more forested landscape
OPEN QUESTION: How many different species lived around Sterkfontein, and how did climate shifts and interbreeding shape them?
